L19: # Transpiler
L20: 
L21: `qiskit.transpiler`
L22: 
L23: * * *
L24: ## Overview
L25: 
L26: Note
L27: 
L28: If you are already familiar with the concepts of circuit transpilation / compilation, you may want to skip ahead to:
L29: 
L30:   * 【11†Descriptions of the preconfigured pass managers】. This includes descriptions of the stages, and of all the available built-in plugins.
L31:   * 【12†Documentation on building a custom transpiler pass】.
L32: Transpilation is the process of rewriting a given input circuit to match the topology of a specific quantum device, and/or to optimize the circuit for execution on quantum systems.
L33: Most circuits must undergo a series of transformations that make them compatible with a given target device, and optimize them to reduce the effects of noise on the resulting outcomes. Rewriting quantum circuits to match hardware constraints and optimizing for performance can be far from trivial. The flow of logic in the rewriting tool chain need not be linear, and can often have iterative sub-loops, conditional branches, and other complex behaviors.
L34: That being said, the standard compilation flow follows the structure given below:
L35: 【13†Image: The transpilation process takes the input circuit, applies the transpilation passes, then produces the output circuit.】
L36: Qiskit uses the graph-based 【14†`DAGCircuit`】 intermediate representation (IR) of a circuit throughout the transpiler stack, rather than the tree-based 【15†`QuantumCircuit`】. A transpiler pipeline is a 【16†`PassManager`】 object, whose 【17†`PassManager.run()`】 method takes in a 【15†`QuantumCircuit`】 and converts it to a 【14†`DAGCircuit`】, then subjects the IR to a sequence of passes, finally returning a 【15†`QuantumCircuit`】 back.
L37: A pass is either an 【18†`AnalysisPass`】, which calculates and stores properties about the circuit in the stateful 【19†`PropertySet`】, or a 【20†`TransformationPass`】, which modifies the IR to achieve a particular singular goal. You can think of a pipeline as being split into “stages”, where each stage is responsible for one high-level transformation.
L38: Qiskit exposes a default transpilation pipeline builder using the function 【21†`generate_preset_pass_manager()`】. This returns a properly configured pipeline for complete transpilation, at a chosen `optimization_level` (between 0 and 3, inclusive). Unless you are looking for something highly specialized, this is almost certainly the entry point you want. A sample transpilation looks like:
L39: 
L40:     `from qiskit.circuit import QuantumCircuit
L41:     from qiskit.transpiler import generate_preset_pass_manager
L42:     from qiskit_ibm_runtime import QiskitRuntimeService
L43: 
L44:     # Any abstract circuit you want:
L45:     abstract = QuantumCircuit(2)
L46:     abstract.h(0)
L47:     abstract.cx(0, 1)
L48: 
L49:     # Any method you like to retrieve the backend you want to run on:
L50:     backend = QiskitRuntimeService().backend("some-backend")
L51: 
L52:     # Create the pass manager for the transpilation ...
L53:     pm = generate_preset_pass_manager(backend=backend)
L54:     # ... and use it (as many times as you like).
L55:     physical = pm.run(abstract)`
L56: For early experiments towards fault tolerance, the functions 【21†`generate_preset_pass_manager()`】 and 【22†`transpile()`】 invoke a specialized transpilation pipeline when the target basis consists of Clifford+T gates, see 【23†`generate_preset_clifford_t_pass_manager()`】 for documentation. It is recommended to use the latter for a detailed configuration of Clifford+T pipelines.
L57: For example, the $R_Z$R Z​ synthesis accuracy cannot be set via `"unitary_synthesis_method"` in 【21†`generate_preset_pass_manager()`】 but can only be globally set via the `"approximation_degree"`. However, 【23†`generate_preset_clifford_t_pass_manager()`】 exposes `"rz_synthesis_config"` for this matter.
L58: For example:
L59: 
L60:     `from qiskit.circuit import QuantumCircuit
L61:     from qiskit.circuit.library import QFTGate
L62:     from qiskit.transpiler import generate_preset_pass_manager
L63:     from qiskit.quantum_info import get_clifford_gate_names
L64: 
L65:     # Any abstract circuit you want:
L66:     abstract = QuantumCircuit(4)
L67:     abstract.append(QFTGate(4), [0, 1, 2, 3])
L68: 
L69:     # Use all Clifford+T basis gates
L70:     basis_gates = get_clifford_gate_names() + ["t", "tdg"]
L71: 
L72:     # Create and run the pass manager
L73:     pm = generate_preset_pass_manager(basis_gates=basis_gates)
L74:     transpiled = pm.run(abstract)`
L75: For most use cases, this is all you need. All of Qiskit’s transpiler infrastructure is highly extensible and configurable, however. The rest of this page details how to harness the low-level capabilities of the transpiler stack.
L76: 
L77: * * *
L78: ## Preset pass managers
L79: 
L80: The function 【21†`generate_preset_pass_manager()`】 creates the “preset pass managers”. These are all instances of 【16†`PassManager`】, so are used by passing a 【15†`QuantumCircuit`】 to the 【17†`PassManager.run()`】 method. More specifically, the preset pass managers are instances of 【24†`StagedPassManager`】, which allows greater configuration of the individual stages of a transpilation, including pre- and post-stage hooks.
L81: A preset pass manager has up to six named stages. These are summarized, in order of execution, below, with more in-depth information in the following subsections.
L82: 
L83: `init`
L84: 
L85: Abstract-circuit optimizations, and reduction of multi-qubit operations to one- and two-qubit operations. See 【25†Initialization stage】 for more details.
L86: 
L87: `layout`
L88: Choose an initial mapping of virtual qubits to physical qubits, including expansion of the circuit to contain explicit ancillas. This stage sometimes subsumes `routing`. See 【26†Layout stage】 for more details.
L89: 
L90: `routing`
L91: Insert gates into the circuit to ensure it matches the connectivity constraints of the 【27†`Target`】. The inserted gates need not match the target ISA yet, so are often just `swap` instructions. This stage is sometimes omitted, when the `layout` stage handles its job. See 【28†Routing stage】 for more details.
L92: 
L93: `translation`
L94: 
L95: Convert all gates in the circuit to ones matching the ISA of the 【27†`Target`】. See 【29†Translation stage】 for more details.
L96: 
L97: `optimization`
L98: Low-level, hardware-aware optimizations. Unlike the abstract optimizations of the `init` stage, this stage acts on a physical circuit. See 【30†Optimization stage】 for more details.
L99: 
L100: `scheduling`
L101: 
L102: Insert 【31†`Delay`】 instructions to make the wall-clock timing of a circuit explicit. This may also include hardware-aware online error reduction techniques such as dynamical decoupling, which are dependent on knowing wall-clock timings. See 【32†Scheduling stage】 for more details.
L103: The preset transpiler pipelines can also be configured at a high level by setting an `optimization_level`. This is an integer from 0 to 3, inclusive, indicating the relative effort to exert in attempting to optimize the circuit for the hardware. Level 0 disables all unnecessary optimizations; only transformations needed to make the circuit runnable are used. On the other end, level 3 enables a full range of optimization techniques, some of which can be very expensive in compilation time.

L18: # ECRGate
L19: 
L20: class `qiskit.circuit.library.ECRGate(*args, _force_mutable=False, **kwargs)`
L21: 
L22: 【11†GitHub†github.com】
L23: 
L24: Bases: 【12†`SingletonGate`】
L25: 
L26: An echoed cross-resonance gate.
L27: 
L28: This gate is maximally entangling and is equivalent to a CNOT up to single-qubit pre-rotations. The echoing procedure mitigates some unwanted terms (terms other than ZX) to cancel in an experiment. More specifically, this gate implements $\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}(IX-XY)$2​1​(I X−X Y).
L29: Can be applied to a 【13†`QuantumCircuit`】 with the 【14†`ecr()`】 method.
L30: 
L31: Circuit symbol:
L32: 
L33:     `                       global phase: 7π/4
L34:          ┌─────────┐            ┌───┐      ┌───┐
L35:     q_0: ┤0        ├       q_0: ┤ S ├───■──┤ X ├
L36:          │   ECR   │   =        ├───┴┐┌─┴─┐└───┘
L37:     q_1: ┤1        ├       q_1: ┤ √X ├┤ X ├─────
L38:          └─────────┘            └────┘└───┘`
L39: 
L40: Matrix representation:
L41: $$ECR\ q_0, q_1 = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}
L42: \begin{pmatrix}
L43: 0   & 1   &  0  & i \\
L44: 1   & 0   &  -i & 0 \\
L45: 0   & i   &  0  & 1 \\
L46: -i  & 0   &  1  & 0
L47: \end{pmatrix}$$E C R q 0​,q 1​=2​1​​0 1 0−i​1 0 i 0​0−i 0 1​i 0 1 0​​
L48: 
L49: Note
L50: In Qiskit’s convention, higher qubit indices are more significant (little endian convention). In the above example we apply the gate on (q_0, q_1) which results in the $X \otimes Z$X⊗Z tensor order. Instead, if we apply it on (q_1, q_0), the matrix will be $Z \otimes X$Z⊗X:
L51: 
L52:     `     ┌─────────┐
L53:     q_0: ┤1        ├
L54:          │   ECR   │
L55:     q_1: ┤0        ├
L56:          └─────────┘`
L57: $$ECR\ q_0, q_1 = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}
L58: \begin{pmatrix}
L59: 0   & 0   &  1  & i \\
L60: 0   & 0   &  i  & 1 \\
L61: 1   & -i  &  0  & 0 \\
L62: -i  & 1   &  0  & 0
L63: \end{pmatrix}$$E C R q 0​,q 1​=2​1​​0 0 1−i​0 0−i 1​1 i 0 0​i 1 0 0​​
L64: 
L65: Parameters
L66: 
L67: label – An optional label for the gate.
L68: 
L69: * * *
L70: ## Attributes
L71: ### base_class
L72: 
L73: Get the base class of this instruction. This is guaranteed to be in the inheritance tree of `self`.
L74: The “base class” of an instruction is the lowest class in its inheritance tree that the object should be considered entirely compatible with for _all_ circuit applications. This typically means that the subclass is defined purely to offer some sort of programmer convenience over the base class, and the base class is the “true” class for a behavioral perspective.
L75: In particular, you should not override 【15†`base_class`】 if you are defining a custom version of an instruction that will be implemented differently by hardware, such as an alternative measurement strategy, or a version of a parametrized gate with a particular set of parameters for the purposes of distinguishing it in a 【16†`Target`】 from the full parametrized gate.
L76: This is often exactly equivalent to `type(obj)`, except in the case of singleton instances of standard-library instructions. These singleton instances are special subclasses of their base class, and this property will return that base. For example:
L77: 
L78:     `>>> isinstance(XGate(), XGate)
L79:     True
L80:     >>> type(XGate()) is XGate
L81:     False
L82:     >>> XGate().base_class is XGate
L83:     True`
L84: In general, you should not rely on the precise class of an instruction; within a given circuit, it is expected that `Instruction.name` should be a more suitable discriminator in most situations.
L85: ### decompositions
L86: 
L87: Get the decompositions of the instruction from the SessionEquivalenceLibrary.
L88: 
L89: ### definition
L90: 
L91: Return definition in terms of other basic gates.
L92: 
L93: ### label
L94: 
L95: Return instruction label
L96: 
L97: ### mutable
L98: 
L99: Is this instance is a mutable unique instance or not.
L100: 
L101: If this attribute is `False` the gate instance is a shared singleton and is not mutable.
L102: 
L103: ### name
L104: 
L105: Return the name.
L106: 
L107: ### num_clbits
L108: 
L109: Return the number of clbits.
L110: 
L111: ### num_qubits
L112: 
L113: Return the number of qubits.
L114: ### params
L115: 
L116: The parameters of this `Instruction`. Ideally these will be gate angles.
L117: 
L118: * * *
L119: 
L120: ## Methods
L121: 
L122: ### add_decomposition
L123: 
L124: `add_decomposition(decomposition)`
L125: 
L126: 【17†GitHub†github.com】
L127: 
L128: Add a decomposition of the instruction to the SessionEquivalenceLibrary.
L129: ### broadcast_arguments
L130: 
L131: `broadcast_arguments(qargs, cargs)`
L132: 
L133: 【18†GitHub†github.com】
L134: 
L135: Validation and handling of the arguments and its relationship.
L136: 
L137: For example, `cx([q[0],q[1]], q[2])` means `cx(q[0], q[2]); cx(q[1], q[2])`. This method yields the arguments in the right grouping. In the given example:
L138: 
L139:     `in: [[q[0],q[1]], q[2]],[]
L140:     outs: [q[0], q[2]], []
L141:           [q[1], q[2]], []`
L142: 
L143: The general broadcasting rules are:
L144: >   * If len(qargs) == 1:
L145: >
L146: >     `[q[0], q[1]] -> [q[0]],[q[1]]`
L147: >
L148: >   * If len(qargs) == 2:
L149: >
L150: >     `[[q[0], q[1]], [r[0], r[1]]] -> [q[0], r[0]], [q[1], r[1]]
L151: >     [[q[0]], [r[0], r[1]]]       -> [q[0], r[0]], [q[0], r[1]]
L152: >     [[q[0], q[1]], [r[0]]]       -> [q[0], r[0]], [q[1], r[0]]`
L153: >
L154: >   * If len(qargs) >= 3:
L155: >
L156: >     `[q[0], q[1]], [r[0], r[1]],  ...] -> [q[0], r[0], ...], [q[1], r[1], ...]`
L157: 
L158: Parameters
L159:   * qargs (【19†list†docs.python.org】) – List of quantum bit arguments.
L160:   * cargs (【19†list†docs.python.org】) – List of classical bit arguments.
L161: 
L162: Returns
L163: 
L164: A tuple with single arguments.
L165: 
L166: Raises
L167: 
L168: 【20†CircuitError】 – If the input is not valid. For example, the number of arguments does not match the gate expectation.
L169: 
L170: Return type
L171: 
L172: 【21†Iterable†docs.python.org】[【22†tuple†docs.python.org】[【19†list†docs.python.org】, 【19†list†docs.python.org】]]
L173: ### control
L174: 
L175: `control(num_ctrl_qubits=1, label=None, ctrl_state=None, annotated=None)`
L176: 
L177: 【23†GitHub†github.com】
L178: 
L179: Return the controlled version of itself.
L180: 
L181: The controlled gate is implemented as 【24†`ControlledGate`】 when `annotated` is `False`, and as 【25†`AnnotatedOperation`】 when `annotated` is `True`.
L182: 
L183: Deprecated since version 2.3
L184: `qiskit.circuit.gate.Gate.control()`’s argument `annotated` is deprecated as of Qiskit 2.3. It will be removed in Qiskit 3.0. The method Gate.control() no longer accepts annotated=None. The new default is annotated=True, which represents the controlled gate as an AnnotatedOperation (unless a dedicated controlled-gate class already exists). You can explicitly set annotated=False to preserve the previous behavior.
L185: However, using annotated=True is recommended, as it defers construction of the controlled circuit to transpiler, and furthermore enables additional controlled-gate optimizations (typically leading to higher-quality circuits).
L186: Parameters
L187:   * num_ctrl_qubits (【26†int†docs.python.org】) – Number of controls to add. Defaults to `1`.
L188:   * label (【27†str†docs.python.org】 | None) – Optional gate label. Defaults to `None`. Ignored if the controlled gate is implemented as an annotated operation.
L189:   * ctrl_state (【26†int†docs.python.org】 |【27†str†docs.python.org】 | None) – The control state of the gate, specified either as an integer or a bitstring (e.g. `"110"`). If `None`, defaults to the all-ones state `2**num_ctrl_qubits - 1`.
L190:   * annotated (【28†bool†docs.python.org】 | None) – Indicates whether the controlled gate should be implemented as a controlled gate or as an annotated operation. If `None`, treated as `False`.
L191: Returns
L192: 
L193: A controlled version of this gate.
L194:

L19: # Fake Provider
L20: 
L21: `qiskit_ibm_runtime.fake_provider`
L22: 
L23: * * *
L24: ## Overview
L25: 
L26: The fake provider module contains fake providers and fake backends classes. The fake backends are built to mimic the behaviors of IBM Quantum systems using system snapshots. The system snapshots contain important information about the quantum system such as coupling map, basis gates, qubit properties (T1, T2, error rate, etc.) which are useful for testing the transpiler and performing noisy simulations of the system.
L27: 
L28: * * *
L29: ## Example Usage
L30: Here is an example of using a fake backend for transpilation and simulation.
L31: 
L32:     `from qiskit import QuantumCircuit
L33:     from qiskit import transpile
L34:     from qiskit.visualization import plot_histogram
L35:     from qiskit_ibm_runtime import SamplerV2
L36:     from qiskit_ibm_runtime.fake_provider import FakeManilaV2
L37: 
L38:     # Get a fake backend from the fake provider
L39:     backend = FakeManilaV2()
L40: 
L41:     # Create a simple circuit
L42:     circuit = QuantumCircuit(3)
L43:     circuit.h(0)
L44:     circuit.cx(0,1)
L45:     circuit.cx(0,2)
L46:     circuit.measure_all()
L47:     circuit.draw('mpl', style="iqp")`
L48: 【11†Image: Circuit diagram output by the previous code.】
L49: 
L50:     `# Transpile the ideal circuit to a circuit that can be
L51:     # directly executed by the backend
L52:     transpiled_circuit = transpile(circuit, backend)
L53:     transpiled_circuit.draw('mpl', style="iqp")`
L54: 【12†Image: Circuit diagram output by the previous code.】
L55: 
L56:     `# Run the transpiled circuit using the simulated fake backend
L57:     sampler = SamplerV2(backend)
L58:     job = sampler.run([transpiled_circuit])
L59:     pub_result = job.result()[0]
L60:     counts = pub_result.data.meas.get_counts()
L61:     plot_histogram(counts)`
L62: 
L63: 【13†Image: Histogram output by the previous code.】
L64: 
L65: Important
L66: Please note that the simulation is done using a noise model generated from system snapshots obtained in the past (sometimes a few years ago) and the results are not representative of the latest behaviors of the real quantum system that the fake backend is mimicking. If you want to run noisy simulations with the latest backend snapshots, you can use the `refresh()` method.
L67: 
L68:     `from qiskit_ibm_runtime import QiskitRuntimeService
L69:     from qiskit_ibm_runtime.fake_provider import FakeSherbrooke
L70:     # initialize service to access real backends
L71:     service = QiskitRuntimeService()
L72: 
L73:     # call refresh to retrieve latest backend data
L74:     # note that this overwrites your local qiskit-ibm-runtime files
L75:     backend = FakeSherbrooke()
L76:     backend.refresh(service)`
L77: * * *
L78: ## Fake Providers
L79: 
L80: Fake providers provide access to a list of fake backends.

L88: ## Fake Backends
L89: ### Fake V2 Backends
L90:
